question: Can compositional tensor summaries approximate symbolic-program output distributions well enough to train neural perception modules when exact weighted model counting or sampling no longer scales?

key_findings.claim: CTSketch converts program inference into a composition of compact tensor contractions rather than enumerating proofs or learning a separate inference network.
key_findings.evidence: The symbolic program is manually decomposed into subprograms. Each subprogram's truth table is encoded as an output-valued tensor, compressed with a low-rank sketch such as Tensor Train, and contracted with incoming categorical distributions; an RBF representation supports numeric outputs and gradients propagate end to end.

key_findings.claim: The approximation analysis bounds downstream distribution error in terms of local tensor-approximation error, but does not make a task-accuracy guarantee.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 3.2 propagates an entrywise tensor error through contractions weighted by input probabilities. This explains when accurate subprogram sketches preserve output probabilities; learned perception error, rank selection, decomposition quality, and optimization remain outside the theorem.

key_findings.claim: The approach extends weak end-to-end supervision to inputs far beyond the tested reach of prior neurosymbolic learners.
key_findings.evidence: On MNIST sum, CTSketch is the only method tested successfully through 1,024 input digits and reports 93.69% inferred per-digit accuracy there. Output accuracy is only 2.73% because every digit must be correct; the analytical reference is 0.003%, while competing learned methods report about 0.6–1.21% but do not recover individual digits meaningfully.

key_findings.claim: Across eleven tasks, CTSketch trades a small amount of peak accuracy for much more consistent scalability and inference speed.
key_findings.evidence: It is best on four reported tasks, is within 2.55 points of A-NeSI on visual Sudoku 4x4 and within 5.42 points of the reference on all multi-digit-addition tasks. For add15, CTSketch averages 1.70 seconds per epoch versus 23.07 for IndeCateR, 52.72 for A-NeSI, and more than 20 minutes for DeepSoftLog.

key_findings.claim: Sketch rank and decomposition introduce non-monotone accuracy, runtime, and memory trade-offs.
key_findings.evidence: On handwritten formulas, rank 8 reaches roughly 95% in 70 minutes while full rank remains near 80% after 90 minutes; rank 4 is smaller but slower to reach 90%. Tensor Train is competitive rather than uniformly best, and CP collapses to 72.90±17.40% on the same task. The authors attribute some reversal of decomposition benefits under sketches to the RBF layer.

key_findings.claim: Manual symbolic engineering and full tensor construction remain the main barriers to broad use.
key_findings.evidence: Every scalable task requires a hand-designed subprogram decomposition, the supported language is restrictive, and the current implementation initializes full tensors before sketching them. The paper explicitly proposes automated decomposition and streaming sketches as future work.

method.core_idea: Exploit program compositionality twice: break a large symbolic map into small maps, then compress each map's tensor representation so approximate weighted inference becomes ordinary differentiable tensor algebra.
method.mechanism: For each subprogram, enumerate a tensor whose input axes index discrete arguments and whose output encodes the program result, optionally through an RBF kernel. Apply a low-rank Tensor-Train decomposition, contract it with perception-model distributions, and feed the resulting distribution into subsequent subprogram tensors. Train only the perception model from terminal labels while propagating gradients through all contractions.
assumptions: The symbolic program is deterministic or can be represented by the paper's one-to-many tensor encoding.
Inputs have finite categorical supports small enough for local subprogram tensors to be constructed.
A useful low-rank approximation exists at practical sketch rank.
A human can decompose the program into subprograms whose intermediate domains remain manageable.

techniques.role: Represents each symbolic subprogram as a differentiable map from input distributions to an output distribution.
Compresses exponentially large truth-table tensors into contracted low-rank cores.
Turns numeric program outputs into smooth categorical-like distributions for composition and training.
Backpropagates only final task labels through fixed symbolic summaries into neural predictors.

evaluations.setting: MNIST sum with 4 to 1,024 digit inputs
evaluations.metric: Exact output accuracy and inferred per-digit accuracy
evaluations.result: At sum1024, CTSketch reports 2.73±0.81% exact-sum accuracy and 93.69% per-digit accuracy; other baselines error, time out, or remain near 0.6–1.21% output accuracy.
evaluations.baseline: Scallop, DeepSoftLog, IndeCateR, ISED, A-NeSI, and a 0.99-per-digit reference

evaluations.result: CTSketch scores 23.5±4.9% on add100, near DeepSoftLog's 25.6±3.4% and above the 13.40% analytical reference; A-NeSI errors and sampling methods fall to 0–6.4%.
evaluations.baseline: DeepSoftLog, IndeCateR, ISED, A-NeSI, Scallop, and reference

evaluations.setting: Visual Sudoku, Sudoku solving, handwritten formulas, leaf and scene tasks
evaluations.result: CTSketch is highest on visual Sudoku 9x9, Sudoku solving, and scene classification in Table 3, and remains competitive rather than best on all tasks.
evaluations.baseline: Scallop, IndeCateR, ISED, and A-NeSI where applicable

evaluations.setting: add15/add100 runtime on one RTX 3090 workstation
evaluations.result: CTSketch averages 1.70 seconds per epoch on add15 and 0.92 on add100; it converges before some exact/neural-inference baselines finish one epoch.
Rank 8 gives the best observed time/accuracy compromise; CP is unstable on HWF while Tensor Train, Tucker, and Tensor Ring cluster around 95.2–95.5% with different memory costs.
evaluations.baseline: Full-rank tensor and alternative CP, Tucker, Tensor Ring decompositions

limitations: Program decomposition is manual and task-specific.
The language assumes finite, tensorizable intermediate domains and is not a general programming language.
Full tensors are materialized before compression, so initialization can fail before the sketch provides savings.
The formal bound controls tensor-output error, not end-task generalization or optimization.
Runtime results use one hardware configuration and task-specific baseline hyperparameters and timeouts.
RBF encodings can make deeper sketched decompositions slower or less accurate.
failure_modes: A subprogram with high tensor rank can erase the expected compression advantage.
Approximation errors can compound across many composed layers despite small local errors.
An unnatural decomposition can create huge intermediate domains or weak gradients.
Terminal labels may be too ambiguous to identify accurate neural inputs, as the A-NeSI sum1024 analysis illustrates for output-only success.
Full-tensor initialization can exhaust memory on exactly the programs for which sketching is most needed.
reusable_insights: Factor a symbolic computation before approximating it; structural factorization can matter more than the approximation family.
Report latent/per-input accuracy alongside terminal accuracy when many component errors collapse into one output label.
Separate the cost of building a compressed representation from the cost of using it.
Benchmark rank selection, decomposition depth, and tensor format jointly because their effects are not monotone.
open_questions: Can streaming or query-only tensor sketches avoid ever materializing full subprogram truth tables?
Can program analysis automatically choose decompositions and ranks with end-to-end error guarantees?
How do approximation errors accumulate over deep or cyclic symbolic programs?
Can the method support continuous, stochastic, stateful, or dynamically branching programs?
What evaluation detects terminal-label shortcuts that do not recover correct latent symbols?

competitive_landscape.title: A-NeSI: A Scalable Approximate Method for Probabilistic Neurosymbolic Inference
competitive_landscape.difference: A-NeSI trains an auxiliary neural network to approximate weighted model counting and can enforce logical constraints. CTSketch fixes an algebraic approximation derived from program tensors, adding a local error analysis and avoiding auxiliary inference-model training but requiring tensorizable decomposition.

competitive_landscape.title: Data-Efficient Learning with Neural Programs
competitive_landscape.difference: ISED estimates learning signals from input-output samples of arbitrary black-box components, including APIs. CTSketch is much more structurally restrictive but replaces sampling variance with fast differentiable contractions.

competitive_landscape.title: DeepProbLog: Neural Probabilistic Logic Programming
competitive_landscape.difference: DeepProbLog integrates neural predicates with exact probabilistic-logic inference, whose proof/counting cost can grow exponentially. CTSketch approximates fixed subprogram semantics with low-rank tensors and also supports non-logic black-box programs when they can be enumerated.

competitive_landscape.title: Scallop: From Probabilistic Deductive Databases to Scalable Differentiable Reasoning
competitive_landscape.difference: Scallop controls proof aggregation through provenance semirings in a Datalog-like language. CTSketch does not enumerate proofs during training and scales better on the paper's large sum tasks, but loses Scallop's declarative logic machinery.

competitive_landscape.title: A Fast Convoluted Story: Scaling Probabilistic Inference for Integer Arithmetic
competitive_landscape.difference: The convolutional approach exploits arithmetic structure and FFTs to accelerate exact probabilistic inference for integer operations. CTSketch is a broader approximate template for decomposable programs, trading exactness and automatic arithmetic specialization for general tensor summaries.

novelty_assessment: CTSketch's substantive novelty is the combination of manually compositional program tensors with low-rank sketches as a fixed, differentiable approximate inference engine. Tensor decompositions and neurosymbolic weighted inference are established separately; the contribution is their integration, a local approximation bound, and unusually large weak-supervision demonstrations. General-purpose scalability is limited by manual decomposition and full-tensor initialization.
reviewer_notes: Read all 18 extracted pages, including the theorem and proof appendix, task-specific decompositions, complete result tables, rank/decomposition/tensor-format ablations, licenses, and stated limitations. Primary arXiv records for A-NeSI and ISED and official paper records for the other baselines were checked on 2026-08-23. The sum1024 result is deliberately separated into 2.73% exact-output accuracy and 93.69% inferred per-digit accuracy to avoid repeating the paper's potentially misleading shorthand.
